L188: # A Look at the Wider Divide in Credit Card Delinquency by Income
L189: 
L190: Donghoon Lee, Daniel Mangrum, Joelle W. Scally, Tejas Sinha, and Wilbert van der Klaauw
L191: 
L192: 【149†Image: Woman sitting at a diningroom table holding a credit card as she looks at her computer. invoices are on the table near her. One has past due on it. She looks worried.】
L193: Credit card delinquency rose sharply between 2022 and 2024, and the increase was steepest among borrowers in lower-income neighborhoods. Here, we check in on credit card performance by neighborhood income and trace when the borrowers who are now struggling with their payments were issued cards. We find that during the pandemic, an increasing share of new credit cards went to borrowers with lower incomes and credit scores, and those accounts are now showing higher levels of distress.
L194: This analysis accompanies the latest 【150†Quarterly Report on Household Debt and Credit†www.newyorkfed.org】, by the New York Fed’s 【101†Center for Microeconomic Data†www.newyorkfed.org】. The report shows that total nominal household debt balances increased by $334 billion in the third quarter of 2026, a 1.8 percent increase from the second quarter of 2026.
L195: Although delinquency rates for mortgages worsened slightly, transition rates into serious delinquency were largely unchanged across non-housing debt types.
L196: Note: The Quarterly Report and this analysis are based on the New York Fed Consumer Credit Panel, which is drawn from anonymized Equifax credit reports.
L197: #### A Widening Gap by Neighborhood Income
L198: We begin our analysis by showing trends in the rate of newly delinquent credit card balances segmented by quartiles of average zip code income. These 【151†delinquency rates declined for all groups†www.federalreserve.gov】 and converged during the pandemic, when forbearances, stimulus payments, and reduced consumption led to improved payment behavior. Since 2022, however, this measure of household distress worsened.
L199: Recent delinquency rates are higher than pre-pandemic levels for all groups, and the gap between borrowers living in higher-income neighborhoods and lower-income neighborhoods has expanded.
L200: The Credit Card Delinquency Gap Between Low-Income and High-Income Areas Widened After 2022
L201: 
L202: Flow into serious delinquency
L203: Sources: New York Fed Consumer Credit Panel/Equifax, IRS Statistics of Income 2022, Census Bureau.
L204: Notes: Zip income quartile (1 = lowest). The flow into serious delinquency is defined as the percent of balance not 90+ days past due in the previous quarter that became 90+ days past due in the current quarter, shown as a four-quarter moving sum. Borrowers are divided into four quartiles of equal population by the mean adjusted gross income in their zip code.
L205: 【152†As previously noted】, this surge partially represents a reversal of pandemic-era dynamics: federal economic stimulus compressed delinquency rates during the pandemic, but today, most households have exhausted their pandemic-era savings and most fiscal and monetary supports have ended. In addition, macroeconomic headwinds —【153†namely high inflation and rising borrowing costs —have squeezed consumers, with inflation outpacing wage growth for low-income brackets】.
L206: #### Loosening Credit Standards During the Pandemic
L207: Although macroeconomic conditions were likely the main contributing factor to the reduction and subsequent increase in delinquency rates, we also explore whether the pandemic-era loosening in credit supply played a role. During the pandemic, 【154†deferments】, 【155†forbearances†www.gao.gov】, and loan modifications contributed to increasing credit scores because many borrowers who would have otherwise been reported past due avoided delinquency.
L208: Concurrently, strong consumer demand combined with low interest rates may have 【156†prompted some lenders to ease underwriting standards and extend credit to those previously not served†www.consumerfinance.gov】.
L209: In the chart below, we plot the share of new credit cards (blue) and new credit limits (red) in each quarter extended to borrowers in the lowest quartile of neighborhood income (the same group comprising the blue line in the first chart). At the start of the pandemic, the share of new cards and credit limits going to these borrowers each rose by nearly 2 percentage points, and the shares remained elevated until 2023, consistent with lenders easing underwriting standards during that period.
L210: #### More Cards and Credit Were Issued to Borrowers in Lower-Income Areas Between 2020-22
L211: 
L212: Share Extended to Borrowers in the Lowest Zip Income Quartile
L213: 
L214: Percent of new originations
L215: Sources: New York Fed Consumer Credit Panel/Equifax, IRS Statistics of Income 2022, Census Bureau.
L216: Notes: The flow into serious delinquency is defined as the percent of balance not 90+ days past due in the previous quarter that became 90+ days past due in the current quarter, shown as a four-quarter moving sum. Borrowers are divided into four quartiles of equal population by the mean adjusted gross income in their zip code.
L217: Evidence from credit scores further confirms this easing. The chart below shows that the median credit score at card issuance fell from an average of 699 in 2017–19 (green region) to 688 during the 2020–22 period (red region). Notably, the decline in median credit score at origination likely understates the extent of easing since credit scores in the population 【157†were generally increasing during the same time†www.fico.com】, as shown in the blue line.
L218: However, this trend reverted toward the end of 2022, similar to the trend in card issuance to low-income areas, with median credit scores for new cards for more recent vintages surpassing the pre-pandemic (green) era.
L219: Pandemic-Era Credit Card Originations Had Lower Credit Scores
L220: 
L221: 【158†Image: LSE_2026_HHDC_credit-card_scally_ch3】Source: New York Fed Consumer Credit Panel/Equifax.
L222: Note: Credit score is Equifax Risk Score 3.0.
L223: Next, we explore how each of these vintages performed given their varied credit quality at issuance. The chart below decomposes our serious delinquency transition rate, the share of balances that became newly 90 or more days delinquent, by the same three vintages in the chart above along with the cards issued prior to 2017. Here we see a similar pattern across most vintages.
L224: Most new delinquencies in each quarter come from more recent vintages, as newly opened “unseasoned” debts have historically been the most likely to fall past due. The cards issued prior to 2017 had already reached their peak delinquency rate by 2018 and were waning in their contribution to the whole throughout the series.
L225: Meanwhile, the 2017-19 vintage reached its relatively low peak during the pandemic era where forbearances and fiscal and monetary supports helped produce historical lows in delinquency. On the other hand, the 2020-22 vintage showed a rapid rise and high peak throughout 2023 and into 2024 where it made up a sizable share of new delinquencies across all vintages, perhaps due to the relatively lower credit quality of this vintage.
L226: Notably, cards issued since early 2023 have generally gone to borrowers with higher scores.
L227: The Effect of the Pandemic-Era Vintage is Waning
L228: 
L229: 【159†Image: LSE_2026_HHDC_credit-card_scally_ch4】Note: The value of each bin is calculated as the balance of loans originated in the corresponding 3-year vintage that is newly 90+ days delinquency in the current quarter divided by the total balance across all vintages that was not 90+ days delinquent in the previous quarter, annualized using a four-quarter moving sum.
L230: Source: New York Fed Consumer Credit Panel/Equifax.
L231: #### What Does This Mean for Delinquency Rates Moving Forward?
L232: 
L233: Delinquency rates for cards issued during the pandemic are abating. If current patterns hold, the elevated delinquencies of the past few years may prove to be more of a pandemic-era echo than a permanent feature of the credit card market—one that may continue to fade as 2020-22 vintages make up a shrinking (and positively selected) share of “surviving” cards.
L234: Of course, since newer cards are more likely to fall past due, the largest factor for near-term delinquency rates is the credit quality of the most recently issued cards. Thus far through 2025, the credit quality of new issuances, as captured by origination credit scores, is below that of 2024 but above the levels of the pre-pandemic and pandemic eras.
L235: So, absent macroeconomic shocks, we anticipate that new credit card delinquencies will likely continue to see signs of improvement, and we will continue to monitor the trends in card performance in the coming quarters.

L318: About the Blog
L319: 
L320: Liberty Street Economics features insight and analysis from New York Fed economists working at the intersection of research and policy. Launched in 2011, the blog takes its name from the Bank’s headquarters at 33 Liberty Street in Manhattan’s Financial District.
L321: The editors are Michael Fleming, Thomas Klitgaard, Maxim Pinkovskiy, and Asani Sarkar, all economists in the Bank’s Research Group.
L322: 
L323: Liberty Street Economics does not publish new posts during the blackout periods surrounding Federal Open Market Committee meetings.
L324: 
L325: The views expressed are those of the authors, and do not necessarily reflect the position of the New York Fed or the Federal Reserve System.

L340: Comment Guidelines
L341: 
L342: 
L343: 
L344: We encourage your comments and queries on our posts and will publish them (below the post) subject to the following guidelines:
L345: Please be brief: Comments are limited to 1,500 characters.
L346: 
L347: Please be aware: Comments submitted shortly before or during the FOMC blackout may not be published until after the blackout.
L348: 
L349: Please be relevant: Comments are moderated and will not appear until they have been reviewed to ensure that they are substantive and clearly related to the topic of the post.
L350: Please be respectful: We reserve the right not to post any comment, and will not post comments that are abusive, harassing, obscene, or commercial in nature. No notice will be given regarding whether a submission will or will
L351: not be posted.‎
L352: 
L353: Comments with links: Please do not include any links in your comment, even if you feel the links will contribute to the discussion. Comments with links will not be posted.
L354: 
L355: Send Us Feedback (research.publications@ny.frb.org)

L357: Disclosure Policy
L358: The LSE editors ask authors submitting a post to the blog to confirm that they have no conflicts of interest as defined by the American Economic Association in its Disclosure Policy. If an author has sources of financial support or other interests that could be perceived as influencing the research presented in the post, we disclose that fact in a statement prepared by the author and appended to the author information at the end of the post.
L359: If the author has no such interests to disclose, no statement is provided. Note, however, that we do indicate in all cases if a data vendor or other party has a right to review a post.
